doc.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Old New Orleans musicians and schooling
title: Who was the best trumpeter; Bunk Johnson's flight and Evan Thomas
summary: Barker rates Buddy Petit highest and tells how Bunk Johnson fled after botching a Mardi Gras job and the story of Evan Thomas's killing in the country.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Who was considered the best trumpet player in New Orleans?

It was Buddy Petit. I’ll tell you that. I never heard Bunk at his heights, but I don’t think Bunk . . . My uncle Paul said Bunk was the greatest, but I think maybe Bud had taken some of the . . . younger than Bunk. Maybe he had something he snatched from Bunk, because Bunk disappeared around 1918, 1919.
Yeah, I think it was the teens.
Yeah, he disappeared. You know why?

Them Jefferson City Buzzards. He blew them up on a Mardi Gras day. He forgot the dates, but took the deposit, and they paraded without a band. They swore that if they caught him, they would put him in a sack and throw him in the Mississippi River, and the word got back to him. Bunk split. He went to New Iberia. He had a friend out there, that band out there. What’s his name?
The guy you mentioned had a band, but I don’t know if he came out later. Hypolite Charles? He was out there.
Yeah. Bunk went out there to play with his band. Bunk was supposed to be there the night when he got killed. That’s all hearsay.
Right, and his horn got smashed, and he stopped playing, because he couldn’t get another horn.
Bunk. The story goes that the guy came after he stabbed . . .
. . . Evan Thomas. I think his name was something like John Gibley, or something like that, and he came back . . .

. . . with a gun and stuff, and he smashed . . . All the musicians ran. Jumped out the window, and he smashed all the instruments. Bunk’s trumpet was on the chair or something, and it got smashed up. Let me ask you this, Mr. Barker. You . . . Who were some of the better that you heard in New Orleans before you, before the ’20s, before you were a kid? Like some of the better clarinet players and trombone players.
